title: Wardrobe and Radiators
premise: Sable Lockridge, a nonbinary bridge inspector whose marriage has settled into silent disrepair, finds a box of undelivered letters hidden behind a wardrobe in their late mother's house — letters from a woman named Odile, written over thirty years to a lover who never received them. As Sable reads them aloud to their spouse Marlowe, the letters force a reckoning: Sable's mother spent her life choosing loyalty to a marriage over truth, and Sable has been repeating the pattern. When Sable tracks down the still-living Odile to deliver the letters in person, they must finally say goodbye — to the mother, to the marriage's comfortable silence, and to the self they buried — choosing truth even as time, and Odile's failing memory, run out.
about_author: Ada Nystrom is a former structural draftsman from Duluth, Minnesota, whose fiction examines the quiet load-bearing failures of ordinary lives. Her short work has appeared in small Midwestern literary journals, and this is her second novel.

chapters.title: Expansion Joints
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. On the Harrow Street Bridge, Sable measures a widening crack and thinks about the widening silence at home with Marlowe. A day of precise, unremarkable work ends with a dinner eaten in parallel silence. Emotional beat: the ache of a life maintained but not inhabited.

chapters.title: The Tenant
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. Back at their mother's vacant house to sort the estate, Sable moves through rooms like a stranger with a checklist. Marlowe texts practical questions; Sable answers none of them honestly. Emotional beat: displacement in one's own inheritance.

chapters.title: Behind the Wardrobe
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. Moving the wardrobe to haul it out, Sable finds a cavity in the plaster and inside it a shoebox: forty-one letters, all addressed to an 'Odile Vasseur,' none ever mailed, spanning 1979 to 1994. Emotional beat: the floor of the known world giving way.

chapters.title: Forty-One Undelivered
chapters.summary: Sable's POV, late night. Sable reads the first letters at the kitchen table — a mother they thought they knew writing with a ferocity and tenderness they never witnessed. The handwriting is unmistakably hers. Emotional beat: vertigo of discovering a stranger inside the most familiar person.

chapters.title: What Marlowe Noticed
chapters.summary: Marlowe's POV. Marlowe has watched Sable go quiet for years and recognizes the signs of a secret, remembering when Sable hid smaller things. When Sable finally mentions 'some of Mom's old papers,' Marlowe pretends not to notice the lie. Emotional beat: the loyalty of silence, and its cost.

chapters.title: The Man in the Photographs
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. The letters reveal the marriage everyone praised — Sable's parents' — was itself a wardrobe with something hidden behind it. Sable finds a photograph of their father with Odile and realizes the letters were written to the woman he loved, by his wife. Emotional beat: inheritance as booby trap.

chapters.title: Reading Aloud
chapters.summary: Dual movement, mostly Sable's POV. Unable to keep it alone, Sable reads a letter aloud to Marlowe — the first honest sentence spoken in their kitchen in years. Marlowe listens all the way through and says, 'You've been gone longer than she has.' Emotional beat: the marriage cracks open into speech.

chapters.title: Odile Vasseur
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. Research leads Sable to a care facility two states away: Odile, ninety-one, in the early stages of dementia, alive. The letters were written to a woman who never knew they existed — and the window to tell her is closing. Emotional beat: urgency disguised as a simple address on an envelope.

chapters.title: The Ethics of Mail
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. Sable debates whether delivering the letters serves Odile or only Sable's need for resolution. Marlowe, unexpectedly fierce, argues: 'She has a right to be loved, even late.' Sable packs the box. Emotional beat: justice outside the law — no statute governs a thirty-year debt of truth.

chapters.title: The Drive
chapters.summary: Sable and Marlowe together, alternating POV. A long drive with the box between them; old grievances surface — the years Sable went invisible, the years Marlowe stopped asking why. They argue at a rest stop, honestly, for the first time. Emotional beat: loyalty and truth pulling the marriage in opposite directions.

chapters.title: Lilacs, Out of Season
chapters.summary: Odile's POV, rendered through her fragmenting memory. Odile remembers a woman named Renata Lockridge, a garden, a promise made at a train station in 1978 — but not how it ended. Emotional beat: a mind like a house with rooms going dark.

chapters.title: First Visit
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. Sable introduces themselves as Renata's child; Odile's face lights with recognition of the surname and confusion about the rest. Sable cannot bring themselves to open the box. They leave having said nothing true. Emotional beat: cowardice inherited, recognized, despised.

chapters.title: The Letter That Explains the Others
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. Letter thirty-nine, dated 1994, explains everything: Renata chose to stay, chose the child, chose silence, and chose to hide the letters rather than burn them — 'so that someone, someday, would have to know I was brave once, in my way.' Emotional beat: Sable's mother becomes a full human being, posthumously.

chapters.title: Saying It Out Loud
chapters.summary: Marlowe's POV. At home, Marlowe confronts Sable: the marriage has been Renata's wardrobe, and Marlowe refuses to be the plaster wall hiding someone. Sable, terrified, begins to say the things they've never said — about identity, about fear, about wanting to be seen. Emotional beat: the novel's central confession.

chapters.title: What Stays and What Goes
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. Sable and Marlowe, neither leaving, renegotiate the terms of staying — not a rescue but a rebuild. Sable clears out the mother's house, keeping only the letters and the photograph. Emotional beat: grief and hope occupying the same room.

chapters.title: The Second Visit
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. Sable returns and reads the first letter aloud to Odile. Odile listens, weeps, and calls Renata by a pet name no one living knew. For twenty minutes she is entirely present. Emotional beat: a thirty-year letter finally arriving; a debt of love partially paid.

chapters.title: Odile's Side
chapters.summary: Odile's POV, lucid window. Odile tells Sable her side: she waited at the station; Renata never came; she built a life anyway. 'Tell her I wasn't angry. Tell her I understood.' She asks Sable to read them all, one visit at a time. Emotional beat: forgiveness that costs the forgiver nothing and the survivor everything.

chapters.title: The Goodbye
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. Over successive visits, Odile's memory fails faster; on the last visit she doesn't recognize Sable, and the letters land on her like news of a stranger's beautiful life. Sable says the goodbye aloud anyway — to Odile, to Renata, in a room where only one of them can hear. Emotional beat: time running out, and speaking anyway.

chapters.title: Inspection Report
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. Back on the Harrow Street Bridge, Sable files a report recommending major repair rather than cosmetic patching — and understands they are writing about themselves. The metaphor lands without winking. Emotional beat: the professional language finally telling the personal truth.

chapters.title: The Wardrobe, Empty
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. Sable donates the wardrobe, keeps the wall's cavity open a final day, and stands in the empty house reading the last letter — Renata's unfinished forty-second, addressed to Sable: 'If you found these, you found me.' Emotional beat: a mother's final message delivered at last.

chapters.title: Load-Bearing
chapters.summary: Sable and Marlowe, alternating. The two of them repair the house's cracked wall themselves — badly, visibly, honestly — and talk through what their marriage will be: not invisible, not perfect, owned. Emotional beat: choosing to be owners, not tenants, of their own life.

chapters.title: Out Loud, At Last
chapters.summary: Sable's POV, coda. Months later, Sable reads selected letters aloud at a small community reading, with Odile's niece's blessing, giving Renata's hidden bravery a public existence. The final line of the novel is the final line of the first letter, spoken to a room of strangers. Emotional beat: resolution — truth delivered, late, imperfectly, and completely.
